title: No label
hookLine: many Jews today choose no movement at all

cards: A registration form for a Jewish summer camp. Name, age, allergies. Then a row of little boxes: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist, Other.
A parent sits with the pen above the boxes for a long moment.

The family lights candles most Fridays, goes to a different synagogue depending on who invites them, fasts on Yom Kippur, argues about Israel at dinner, and sends the kids to Hebrew school. None of the boxes fits.
The parent ticks Other and writes, in small letters, just Jewish.

teach.b: No label. Go back to the people before the boxes. When the Israelites leave Egypt, the Torah says, "a mixed multitude went up also with them."
There were no movement names on that road. The streams in this block, from Orthodox to Humanistic, are real and serious, and they are also newer than the people. Then the covenant.
Moses tells the people in Deuteronomy, "Neither with you only do I make this covenant and this oath," but also with those standing there and those not there that day.
In that reading, the covenant comes before any membership list. Now the shape of a no-label life. Some Jews today belong to no movement at all.

teach.h: A LITTLE OF EVERYTHING, AT HOME.
teach.b: They may pray at an Orthodox synagogue on the High Holy Days, take a class at a Reform temple, join a friend's Shabbat dinner, and keep their own customs at home. Some call themselves just Jewish.
Some are simply not interested in the question. Each of the movements would say it offers something a person shouldn't do without: a community, a teacher, a framework that holds when life gets hard.
That is a fair point, and a no-label Jew may well agree and still not pick a box. Last, a line for balance.
Hillel taught, in the Mishnah, do not separate yourself from the community.
No label is not the same as no people. A Jew without a movement can still be counted, still be welcomed, still belong. The label is optional.
The belonging, in Hillel's view, is not.

how: Jews who choose no movement may attend different synagogues for different occasions, study and celebrate with friends, keep customs at home, and describe themselves as just Jewish.

games.q: you're the parent with the camp form. none of the boxes fits your family. what do you do?
o: tick the box closest to what you do.
tick Other and write just Jewish.
leave the form blank and skip camp.
games.why: just Jewish: some Jews choose no movement and describe their practice in their own words.

practice: Silently, in three plain sentences, say what you actually do, not what you call yourself: I light a candle on some evenings. I call my mother on Sundays. Whatever is true.
Then notice how it feels to be described by your actions instead of a box.

wordCard.voice: No label. Jews who belong to no movement, who describe their practice in their own words, and who are still part of the people. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: no label needed. Just Jewish, written in small letters, still counts. See you tomorrow.
